name: Alt-right
summary: A loose, largely online movement of the 2010s, named by Richard Spencer in 2008, that treats white (European) identity as its organising principle. Its leaders (Spencer, Taylor, Anglin, Johnson) reject egalitarianism and liberal democracy, hold that race is real and hereditary, want sharply restricted immigration and racial separation or ethnic states, and break with the conservative establishment. Scholars such as Main read it as a rival to liberal democracy, and May and Feldman as a rebranding of fascism. Its economics and social policy are secondary, so the record on many statements is silent.
scope: The mainstream 'Alternative Right' of about 2008-2018 as the scholarship (Main 2018; May and Feldman) and the movement's leaders define it: Spencer's AlternativeRight.com, Radix and the National Policy Institute, Taylor's American Renaissance, Johnson's Counter-Currents, Anglin's Daily Stormer, Griffin, Kirkpatrick, MacDonald and Brimelow. It excludes the 'alt-lite' civic nationalists (Breitbart, Yiannopoulos), whom Friberg separates from it, paleoconservatism before 2008, and the League of the South's neo-Confederate tradition. Where leaders differ (Spencer's separation, Anglin's removal, Taylor's rejection of the word supremacy) the answer follows what the sources state and says so.

notes: Themes searched: race and ethnicity, immigration, democracy and elections, gender and family, religion, the economy and trade, foreign policy and aid, free speech, culture and metapolitics, in Main (2018), May and Feldman, the UCLA glossary, Hawley's two books (2017, 2019), and Spencer's and Taylor's own interviews in the MediaSum corpus; I also searched Hawley for monarchy, class, alliances, military blocs, secession, authoritarian rule and free speech and found no Alt-Right position on them (his monarchist and technocratic strand is neoreaction, which he separates from the Alt-Right). The movement had no programme: its leaders agree on race, immigration, anti-egalitarianism and opposition to the conservative establishment, and the record is otherwise silent on economics, courts, religion, taxes, the environment, technology and most institutional questions, so these are null. Strands differ (Anglin's removal and Jewish conspiracy against Spencer's separation and Taylor's rejection of the word supremacy); answers state the strand the source gives. Many Wikipedia-based and SPLC-based answers from the first pass were withdrawn because those pages are not evidence. The uncertainty rule may fail on thin lines: that is an honest result.
